analysis.one_liner: Designates the Arctic Refuge coastal plain as wilderness, permanently barring oil drilling there.
analysis.headline: The bill to protect 1.56 million acres of the Arctic Refuge coastal plain as wilderness was introduced in February 2020, sent to two subcommittees, and died without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add about 1,559,538 acres of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coastal plain in Alaska to the National Wilderness Preservation System, to be managed under the Wilderness Act as part of the refuge's existing wilderness [S2] [S3]. Wilderness designation is the strictest land protection in federal law: no roads, no vehicle use, and no oil and gas development. That would permanently block drilling on the coastal plain, the part of the refuge where Congress in 2017 opened the door to oil leasing.
analysis.who_benefits: The American public in general: future generations would keep an untouched Arctic wilderness, and the wildlife, habitats, and wild rivers of the coastal plain would be preserved. The bill's stated purpose is preserving the area 'for the permanent good of present and future generations of Americans' [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone who wants the Arctic Refuge protected

how_it_helps.text: Permanently protects roughly 1,559,538 acres of the Arctic Refuge coastal plain by adding them to the National Wilderness Preservation System, managed under the Wilderness Act alongside the refuge's existing wilderness [S2] [S3].
Because wilderness status bars development, it would foreclose oil and gas leasing and drilling on the coastal plain, the same acreage Congress opened to a leasing program in 2017.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies and pro-drilling interests would lose access to a potentially oil-rich area, and Alaska state and local interests that had counted on drilling revenue would lose that opportunity. No taxpayer cost is created by the designation itself.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil companies seeking Arctic drilling rights

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection is economic: the coastal plain sits above federally estimated oil resources, and drilling proponents argue development would create jobs, royalty payments, and energy supply, much of it flowing to Alaska's economy. Wilderness designation forecloses that option permanently, not just temporarily.

The bill as introduced had no cosponsors, so it represented a single member's position rather than a broadly negotiated proposal, and it never received a hearing where those tradeoffs could be aired in this Congress [S4] [S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit is permanent preservation of the largest protected wilderness area in the United States and a ban on drilling the coastal plain; its cost is giving up potential oil revenue and energy development that would mainly have benefited the oil industry and Alaska's treasury. The tradeoff is genuinely contested, but the bill never got far enough for Congress to weigh it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to two subcommittees, and it sat there until the Congress ended in January 2021 without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Jared Huffman introduced the bill on February 27, 2020, and it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources the same day [S5].
On March 5, 2020, it was referred to the Subcommittee on National Parks, Forests, and Public Lands and to the Subcommittee on Water, Oceans, and Wildlife; no further action followed [S5].
No member joined as a cosponsor during the Congress [S4].
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and all bills not passed expire when a Congress ends.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas interests and drilling advocates are better off: the coastal plain remains open to the leasing program Congress created in 2017, since wilderness protection never came to a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas interests and pro-drilling advocates

for.name: Rep. Jared Huffman
for.role: Sponsor, House Natural Resources Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to designate the Arctic Refuge coastal plain as wilderness.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction; never scheduled a hearing or markup
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from referral in February 2020 through the end of the Congress without acting on it.

against.name: Pro-drilling interests, including Alaska's congressional delegation
against.role: Opponents of wilderness designation for the ANWR coastal plain
against.what_they_did: Long opposed any wilderness designation that would permanently block oil development on the coastal plain, which Congress opened to leasing in 2017.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill drew zero cosponsors, so the partisan shape of support and opposition never showed up in the record [S4].

industries.note: Wilderness status would permanently bar drilling on the coastal plain, an area Congress opened to oil leasing in 2017 and that geologists believe holds significant oil. The bill would have taken that opportunity off the table for good; its death leaves it open.
